reference.question: The marking line of an angled parking space is 6 m long and forms an acute angle of \(30^\circ\) with the driving aisle. How many m of depth does the space occupy perpendicular to the driving aisle?
reference.solution:
Method 1: Use the sine ratio

Depth \(=6\times\sin30^\circ=6\times\frac{1}{2}=3\) m.

Method 2: Use the 30° right-triangle property

Dropping a perpendicular from the far endpoint of the marking line to the aisle forms a right triangle. The 6 m marking line is its hypotenuse, and the depth is the leg opposite \(30^\circ\). In a right triangle, that leg is half the hypotenuse, so the depth is \(6/2=3\) m.

edges.reason: Point-to-point shortest-distance language is a helpful model, but perpendicular-shortest distance is a separate fact and not derived merely from the two-point line axiom.
The distance in question is the length of the perpendicular from the point, so perpendicularity identifies which segment is measured.
An equilateral construction explains the half-hypotenuse theorem, but the actual criteria state and apply it without prescribing a proof. Gemini imports the derivation into an application criterion.
edges.scope: Understanding why the half-hypotenuse property holds

edges.reason: Angle-independent ratios use proportional sides of similar right triangles.
Exact special-angle calculations use irrational square-root values and real arithmetic.
A special trigonometric value is a value of the corresponding side ratio.
Numerical solutions need special-value or calculator evaluation, both covered here.
edges.scope: obtaining trig values to find elements
